1.pericope_label: Josiah’s accession, his early seeking of God, and the purge of Judah and the northern tribes

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch and Ellicott both take the eighth year as the eighth of the reign, making the king sixteen; Keil and Delitzsch call the Chronicle the more exact of the two accounts, since it keeps the events apart and in their order of time while Kings views the whole reform in connection with the finding of the book, and they explain the burning of the priests’ bones as a deliberate defilement of the place with the ashes of the dead, why Simeon is counted among the northern tribes, and why the phrase describing the northern progress is unintelligible as it stands. Ellicott adds that Josiah is the only king of whom it is said he declined neither to the right hand nor to the left, which amounts to saying his observance of the law was perfect, renders the images as sun statues, and confirms from Kings that the king superintended the demolition himself.

Henry presses that Josiah had nothing like Manasseh’s education and may have had about him those who wished to corrupt him, yet sought God early, which is the duty and the honour of the young; he supposes something was done at twelve, that the work met opposition and was not thorough until the book of the law was found six years later, and that the historian has laid the whole together briefly; and on the encomium he observes that there are errors on both hands.

Gill agrees that the king was sixteen but preserves two other readings of the eighth year, has Josiah present in person at the demolition rather than merely issuing orders, notes that these were Manasseh’s altars, cast out at his humiliation and rebuilt by his son, and accounts for the king’s authority in the northern cities by the Assyrian captivity having left the remnant subject to Judah.

Wesley has the king begin to seek God just as he entered the age of temptation, the government in his own hands and none to restrain him; Clarke reads the refusal to decline either way as a double guard, timidity not keeping him from going far enough nor zeal carrying him beyond due bounds, so that he walked in the golden mean.

debates.question: What does the eighth year count from, and when did Josiah begin to seek God?

positions.view: The eighth year of the reign, so that he was sixteen when he began to seek the God of David
The eighth year of his age, that is the year he began to reign
The clause is a concession — that though he was young he began to seek God

debates.question: Why does this account date the purge to the twelfth year where Kings dates the reform to the eighteenth?

positions.view: Something was begun at twelve, met opposition, and was not thorough until the book was found, the whole being laid together briefly
The Chronicle is simply the more exact, keeping the events in their order of time
The extirpation was placed first to show the king needed no prompting
held_by: Thenius (as reported, and rejected, by Charles Ellicott)

positions.view: The order was meant to clear so praised a king of tolerating the abomination for eighteen years
held_by: Noldeke (as reported, and rejected, by Charles Ellicott)

outliers.claim: Alone in supplying the fact that gives the encomium its weight — that no other king is said to have declined neither to the right hand nor to the left.
Alone in reading that formula as a double guard against timidity on one side and excess of zeal on the other.

8.pericope_label: The eighteenth-year repair of the temple: the collection, the faithful workmen, and the musical overseers

schools.summary: Ellicott notes a difference of form rather than substance, that Kings gives this material as the king’s instructions while this account reports them carried out, gives the literal sense that the men were dealing in good faith, recalls that in Kings this is the ground on which the high priest is told to require no account of the money, renders the flooring as raftering and the houses as the chambers, and rejects an attempt to make the collection an organised levy throughout the land. Keil and Delitzsch read the Hebrew text as giving the dwellers in Jerusalem and the marginal reading as a correction arising from a misunderstanding, and judge the enumeration from the hand of Manasseh and Ephraim rhetorical.

Henry marks the order as the pattern — the house cleansed before it is fitted for its services, as the heart must be cleansed before it is renewed into God’s image — notices that Josiah calls God the Lord his God, since those who love God will love the habitation of his house, holds that workmen are not completely faithful unless both careful and diligent because a confidence is reposed in them, and draws from the pairing of labourers and overseers that God dispenses his gifts variously, the one the hands and the other the heads, each needing the other.

Gill reckons the king twenty-six in the eighteenth year, with six years of purging behind him, and has the burden-bearers overseen lest they be dilatory or the workmen stand idle for want of materials.

Clarke holds that for the clause rendered and they returned we should read the inhabitants, a reading supported by many manuscripts and printed editions and all the versions as well as by necessity and common sense; Wesley takes the houses to be the chambers adjoining the temple.

debates.question: Why were the overseers of the work chosen from Levites skilled in music?

positions.view: They played to enliven the workmen, as a recovered Greek treatise on music shows was done for hire in antiquity
They probably did cheer the labour with song, as in ancient Egypt, the term for setting the work forward being itself a musical one
They were exercised in both employments by turns, overseeing the work and praising God with voice and instrument
Their skill in music could be of no use in architecture and is named only as evidence that they were men of sense whose genius lay toward the mathematics

debates.question: Does the clause mean that they returned, or the inhabitants of Jerusalem?

positions.view: The inhabitants, on the weight of manuscripts, editions and versions
The written text gives the dwellers in Jerusalem, and the margin is a correction born of misunderstanding it

outliers.claim: Alone in grounding his answer on a Greek treatise on music recovered from the cities buried beneath Vesuvius, which shows a harper paid from the workmen’s wages to play while they laboured.
Alone in softening the charge against the earlier kings, suggesting that destroyed may mean no more than allowed to go to ruin.

14.pericope_label: The book of the law found; Josiah rends his clothes and sends to enquire of Huldah

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch are careful to say the words do not clearly imply the book was found where the money was laid up, hold that the phrase about Moses characterises it as the book of the Mosaic law and not necessarily as his autograph, and treat the small differences in the account of its delivery as clarifications that make the matter plainer without altering the facts. Ellicott reaches the same conclusion by syntax, holding that the phrase by the hand of Moses attaches not to the book but to the law of Jehovah; he corrects the English article to the book rather than a book, twice refuses to let the wording carry an inference that the volume was bulky, argues that the kindled against of Kings is probably original where this text has the wrath poured out, would restore the defective list of messengers from the versions, settles the variant spellings in Huldah’s genealogy by weighing them, and renders the place she lived not a college but the second quarter, that is the lower city.

Henry begins from what the scene should make a later reader feel — that Bibles are jewels but, thanks be to God, not rarities, the fountain no longer a spring shut up but a stream flowing for common use — and warns that we shall have much to answer for if the great things of God’s law, being made common, come to be accounted strange; on the rent clothes he grants that God was pleased with the gesture yet turns it inward, that these things are not less weighty for being well known, so rend the heart and not the garments; and he takes the chapter to direct us under conviction of sin to enquire of the Lord as Josiah did.

Gill traces only the chain of hands, the Levites bringing the money from the country to the temple, the high priest passing it to the king’s ministers and they to the overseers, so that the repairs began.
Wesley makes the same point as Henry about the rent clothes, and in nearly the same words, that the heart and not the garment is what should be rent.

debates.question: Where in the temple was the book found?

positions.view: The words do not clearly imply it was found where the money was laid up
The high priest found it in the treasure-chamber, which he had entered to fetch gold and silver for making sacred vessels
It had been hidden under a heap of stones to save it from being burnt by Ahaz
held_by: rabbinic tradition (as reported by Charles Ellicott)

debates.question: Is this account’s wording of the oracle an alteration of the older text or a clarification of it?

positions.view: An alteration, and a traceable one: the wrath poured out for kindled against, and the remnant left in Israel for the simpler phrase, both looking back to the ruin of the ten tribes
Clarifications rather than discrepancies, making the matter plainer without altering the facts

outliers.claim: Alone in turning the scene on the later reader, warning that the great things of God’s law, being made common, may come to be accounted strange.

24.pericope_label: Huldah’s oracle: the curses written in the book, and the promise to the king who humbled himself

schools.summary: Ellicott notes that the opening is a participle, so that God is about to bring the evil rather than merely resolved on it, and identifies the curses in view as those of Deuteronomy, which he lists; he finds the hand of the later writer visible throughout the oracle and consistently in one direction — the wrath poured out where Kings has it kindled, which he judges the better reading since it agrees with the promise that it shall not be quenched; the clause about the king humbling himself absent from Kings; the added words about the inhabitants of the place; the grave a plural in the Hebrew — all of which press the theme of humbling that the oracle turns on.

Henry draws the general warning that those who forsake God bring evil on themselves and kindle a fire which shall not be quenched, as the fire of his wrath will be when the decree has gone out against the impenitent; and on the promise he observes that Josiah’s humbling will not turn the wrath from the land yet delivers his own soul, that good people are taught by it to be so far from fearing death as to welcome it when it takes them away from the evil to come, and that the whole property of the thing is altered by being made the matter of a promise — gathered to the grave in peace, housed in that ark as Noah was when a deluge was coming.

Clarke stops at the clause about the tender heart and renders the Targum’s version of it, that the king’s heart was melted and he humbled himself in the sight of the Word of the Lord when he heard his words against this place, pointing out that the paraphrast there uses two different terms, one for the Word as a person and another for a word merely spoken or expressed.

outliers.claim: Alone in reading the clause through the Targum, and in resting on its use of two distinct terms — one for the Word as a person, one for a word merely spoken.

29.pericope_label: The covenant read before the assembled nation, and the people made to stand to it

schools.summary: Henry marks the order of it, that the king did not force the people to their duty until he had instructed them in it, calling great and small, young and old, rich and poor, since all were concerned in the words; that the king read rather than the priests put honour on the service, and Henry supposes he read so as to show he was himself affected, which would affect his hearers; he has both king and people subscribe the articles, the king covenanting in his place and then urging the people to declare their consent; and he judges that all Josiah’s days were days of restraint upon a people with a bent to backslide, many wanting nothing but to have him out of the way, so that nothing hastens the ruin of a people more than the baffling of hopeful attempts at reformation and a hypocritical return to God.

Ellicott explains the substitution of the Levites for the prophets of Kings as natural for a writer in whose day the prophetic order was long extinct, though he allows it may be an unconscious slip; he glosses the king’s standing as on his stand and takes the word Kings uses for the dais to be synonymous; he suspects the verse about the people was disturbed in transmission, since Kings and the Syriac both say they came into the covenant and the verbs for standing and causing to stand differ only in vowels anciently unwritten; and he allows that the royal will secured an outward conformity while calling the unreality of reformations by royal mandate proved by the relapse that followed immediately on Josiah’s death.
Gill notes that from here to the end the account runs as it does in Kings, and takes the clearing of the abominations to cover all the idols already related.

Clarke takes the people’s part physically, that the king likely made them all rise as the terms were read, so testifying their approbation of the covenant and their resolve to keep it faithfully and perseveringly; Wesley takes it as a binding act, that he made them engage by oath or covenant to observe the laws of God as his predecessors had done and as they were already obliged to do, and ends on the doubled verb, that Josiah aimed at nothing else but to engage them to God and their duty.

debates.question: What did Josiah make the people do when the covenant was read?

positions.view: He made them rise to their feet, testifying their approbation and their resolve to keep the covenant
He made them engage by oath or covenant to observe the laws of God
King and people alike subscribed the articles, the king first and then the people declaring their consent
The text has been disturbed, and originally said the people came into the covenant, as Kings and the Syriac have it

outliers.claim: Alone in judging the phrase about Benjamin a likely corruption of the words about entering the covenant, which the sense requires here as much as in Kings.
Alone in dating the iniquity that ruined the house of Judah from the very year of the reformation.
